title: Spared by the feet that humbled him
hook: the serpent's wives plead for his life, and the marks of Krishna's feet become his protection
carry: his lotus feet humble, then protect
tomorrow: Why the village fed a hill

segments.voice: Yesterday the boy danced on Kaliya's hoods until the serpent's pride was gone, and Kaliya remembered the Lord. Your line was he humbles the ego and spares the soul.

The serpent is beaten. He lies broken in the water, the boy still standing on his heads. And out of the pool come the serpent's wives. The Bhagavata calls them the naga wives, and they don't come to fight. They come with their children in front of them, hair loose, clothes disordered, and bow before Krishna with their palms joined. Kaliya can't speak for himself anymore. So they speak for him.
screen: `THE SERPENT IS BEATEN.` → `HIS WIVES COME OUT OF THE POOL.` → `THEY SPEAK FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: What they say is surprising. They don't argue that their husband is innocent. They call his punishment fair, more than fair: a grace. Your feet have touched his head, they say, and others perform long austerities hoping for the dust of those feet. Then they ask one thing: spare him. He is our husband. Let him live. And Krishna lets him go. Kaliya, getting his breath back, speaks plainly. We serpents are born this way, angry by nature, with poison in us. It's hard to let go of what you're made of. Krishna gives him a way forward: leave this pool, go to the ocean with your family, so the river can be clean again for the people and the cows. Then Krishna names the fear that brought Kaliya here. He was hiding. Garuda, the eagle who preys on serpents, could not enter this pool because of a sage's old curse, so this poisoned corner of the Yamuna was the one place he felt safe. And Krishna answers that fear. Garuda won't harm you now, he says, because you carry the marks of my feet on your hoods. So the story ends with no one destroyed. The poison leaves the river, and the feet that broke his pride become his shelter. That's why Hindu devotion speaks so often of the Lord's lotus feet. People bow at the feet of the image in the temple. Many temples give charanamrit, water that has bathed the deity's feet, as a blessing. To take refuge at his feet, as devotees say, means this: what humbles you is also what keeps you safe.
screen: `"YOUR FEET HAVE TOUCHED HIS HEAD."` · `"WE ARE BORN THIS WAY."` · `GO TO THE OCEAN; LET THE RIVER BE CLEAN.` · then, large: `REFUGE AT HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose sharpness you've felt, and gently wonder what they might be afraid of, what corner they crawled into to feel safe. If you pray, picture laying them at Krishna's feet, the way Kaliya's wives did, and asking that they be spared, and sent somewhere better than their poison. If you don't pray, simply wish them a cleaner river to live in.
Kaliya. The serpent spared at his wives' plea, sent to the ocean, and protected by the very footprints that subdued him.
Your line: his lotus feet humble, then protect. Tomorrow, a boy asks his father a question. Day eight hundred ninety-four, done.
